n: After years of stalled work, God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, to stir up the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. Prophetic voices restarted what discouragement had stopped. Their messages are preserved in the books bearing their names.

f.g: Literally grandson of Iddo; his father was Berechiah.

n: Zerubbabel and Jeshua responded and began building again (520 BC), and the prophets were right there helping. Prophets don’t just speak; they stand with the people in the work.

f.w: the prophets of God helping them

n: Tattenai, the Persian governor of the province beyond the Euphrates, and Shethar-bozenai came asking: who authorized you to build this house and finish this structure?

f.g: Tattenai — his name appears in a Babylonian document from 502 BC as governor of the region.
Probably ‘this structure’ — the temple’s woodwork or walls.

n: They also demanded the names of the men responsible for the building. (“We” here likely reflects the source document’s voice.)

f.g: Ancient versions read ‘they said’ — the officials asked.

n: But God’s eye was watching over the Jewish elders, so the officials didn’t stop the work while waiting for Darius’s reply. God’s watchful care allowed the work to continue.

f.w: the eye of their God was upon the elders

n: Here is the copy of the letter Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai, and their officials sent to King Darius. Unlike the hostile letter in chapter 4, this one is fairly neutral and fair.

f.g: Probably a Persian term for officials or investigators.

n: The letter opens with the formal greeting: “To King Darius, all peace.”
They reported that the house of “the great God” in Judea was being built with large stones and timber in the walls, and the work was moving fast and succeeding.

f.g: Literally ‘stones of rolling’ — blocks so large they had to be rolled into place.

n: We asked the elders who gave them permission to build.
We also asked their leaders’ names so we could inform you.
The elders answered with a bold testimony: we are servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding the house a great king of Israel (Solomon) built long ago.

f.w: We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth

n: They honestly admitted their ancestors provoked God, so He handed them to Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed the temple and exiled them. They owned their history.

f.w: our fathers had provoked the God of heaven

f.g: Of the Chaldean dynasty ruling Babylon.

n: But in Cyrus’s first year as king of Babylon, he issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.

f.w: a decree to build this house of God

n: Cyrus also returned the gold and silver temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, giving them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor.
Cyrus told him to take the vessels to Jerusalem and rebuild God’s house on its original site.
Sheshbazzar laid the foundation, and construction had continued — slowly — ever since, but wasn’t finished. (In reality, it had been halted for years.)
The officials asked the king to search the royal archives in Babylon to see whether Cyrus really issued such a decree, and to send his decision. Truth could be verified in the records.

f.g: The royal archives where official records were kept.
